chapters.title: Chapter 6: After Filing: Refunds, Notices and Fixing Mistakes

lessons.title: Belated, Revised and Updated Returns: Deadlines, Fees and When to Use Each

body.text: The law gives you three second chances, and each one is weaker and costlier than the last. A revised return fixes anything. A belated return costs you money and options. An updated return only lets you pay more tax, never claim less.

children.text: Missing the due date is not the end of the road, but which road remains open depends on what went wrong and how late you are. All three routes sit in Section 263 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 139 of the Income-tax Act, 1961): belated returns in sub-section (4), revised returns in (5) and updated returns in (6). Returns for FY 2025-26 still follow the 1961 Act.

cells: Belated return: you never filed on time
Late fee up to ₹5,000, plus 1% a month interest on unpaid tax
Cannot use the old regime, and most losses cannot be carried forward
Revised return: you filed, but something was wrong
31 March 2027, or completion of assessment if earlier
Nothing by itself, beyond tax and interest on any extra income
Cannot be filed if you never filed an original return
Updated return (ITR-U): you left out income
Additional tax of 25% to 70% of tax plus interest
Cannot create or increase a refund, reduce your tax, or report a loss

events.title: Due Date for ITR-1 and ITR-2
events.description: File by this date to keep every option: old regime, loss carry-forward and refund interest from 1 April.

events.title: Due Date for Non-Audit ITR-3 and ITR-4
events.description: The separate date for business and professional filers who need no audit.

events.title: Last Date for a Belated Return
events.description: After this, you cannot file a normal return for the year at all.

events.title: Last Date to Revise
events.description: Any return, filed on time or belated, can be revised until the end of the assessment year.

events.title: Last Date for an Updated Return
events.description: Forty-eight months from the end of the assessment year, but only to declare more income and pay more tax.

children.text: The Belated Return: Late, But Still a Return

If you missed your due date, you can still file until 31 December 2026 for FY 2025-26. Everything works normally: the same forms, the same portal, the same verification. What changes is the price. The late fee under Section 428 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 234F of the 1961 Act) is ₹5,000, reduced to ₹1,000 if your total income is up to ₹5 lakh, and nil if your income is below the basic exemption limit and you were not otherwise required to file.

body.title: What a Belated Return Costs You

columns.label: You Still Get
points: Your refund, if one is due
Credit for all TDS and TCS shown in Form 26AS
The right to revise the belated return until 31 March 2027
A valid ITR acknowledgement for loans and visas
Carry-forward of house property losses

columns.label: You Lose
points: The option to choose the old regime: a belated return is taxed under the new regime
Carry-forward of capital losses and business losses, including F&O losses
Refund interest from 1 April; it runs only from the date of filing
₹5,000 as a late fee, or ₹1,000 for smaller incomes
1% a month interest on unpaid tax from the day after the due date

body.title: What Lateness Costs Deepak
body.prompt: Deepak has a total income of ₹8,00,000 and tax of ₹22,000 still unpaid on the due date. He files his belated return and pays on 10 November 2026, having missed the 31 July 2026 due date. Counting the late fee and the 1% a month late filing interest, with part months counting in full, how much does his delay cost him in total?
body.explanation: The late fee is ₹5,000, because his income is above ₹5 lakh. Late filing interest runs from 1 August to 10 November 2026, which is August, September, October and part of November, so 4 months: ₹22,000 × 1% × 4 = ₹880. Total ₹5,880, on top of the ₹22,000 tax he owed anyway. He also cannot use the old regime this year.

children.text: The Revised Return: The Friendly One

A revised return replaces your earlier return completely. You can use it to add income you forgot, claim a deduction you missed, correct a wrong bank account, or fix the form itself if you filed ITR-1 when you needed ITR-2. There is no fee for revising, you can revise more than once, and even a belated return can be revised. You will need the acknowledgement number and date of the original return, and the revised return must be e-verified like any other.

body.text: For FY 2025-26, the window to revise runs to 31 March 2027, which is later than the 31 December 2026 belated deadline. So if you discover a mistake in January 2027, you can still revise a return you filed, even though nobody can file a fresh return for that year any more.

body.title: Which Route Applies?
body.question: Ritu filed her ITR-1 on 24 July 2026 and it has already been processed. In October 2026 she realises she never reported ₹40,000 of FD interest from a bank she rarely uses. What should she file?
options: A belated return, since the due date has passed
A revised return, paying the extra tax and interest
An updated return, with 25% additional tax
Nothing, because her return was already processed
body.explanation: She filed on time, so the belated route does not apply, and revision is open until 31 March 2027 even after processing. A revised return costs no fee: she pays only the tax on ₹40,000 plus any interest. An updated return would add 25% on top, and is meant for people who no longer have the revision window. Doing nothing is the worst option, since the interest is already in her AIS.

children.text: The Updated Return: Expensive, and One Way Only

markDefs.definition: A return filed to declare income left out of an earlier return, up to 48 months after the end of the assessment year, with additional tax of 25% to 70% of the tax and interest due. It cannot be used to claim a refund or report a loss.

children.text: Once the revision window closes, the only route left is an

, filed in Form ITR-U. The Finance Act, 2025 extended the window from 24 months to 48 months, so for AY 2026-27 you can file until 31 March 2031. It exists for one purpose: letting you come forward with income you did not report, and pay for the privilege.

body.title: Price an Updated Return
body.prompt: Vinod left out freelance income from an earlier year. His recomputed tax on it is ₹40,000 and the interest comes to ₹9,000. He files ITR-U 20 months after the end of that assessment year. What is the total he must pay, including additional tax?
body.explanation: Tax plus interest is ₹40,000 + ₹9,000 = ₹49,000. At 20 months he is in the 12 to 24 month band, so additional tax is 50% of ₹49,000, which is ₹24,500. Total: ₹73,500. Had he come forward within 12 months, the additional tax would have been ₹12,250, saving ₹12,250.

body.text: An updated return is a one-way street. It cannot be filed to claim or increase a refund, to reduce your tax, or to report a loss; it must result in more tax being paid. Only one updated return is allowed per assessment year, and it cannot be withdrawn or corrected once submitted. It is also barred where a search, survey or assessment proceeding is under way for that year.

body.title: Revised vs Updated: The Difference That Costs Money

columns.label: Revised Return
points: Available until 31 March 2027 for AY 2026-27
Needs an original return to have been filed
Can increase or reduce income, and can increase a refund
No additional tax, and can be filed more than once

columns.label: Updated Return
points: Available until 31 March 2031 for AY 2026-27
Can be filed even if you never filed a return for that year
Can only increase income and tax
Additional tax of 25% to 70%, and one attempt only

body.title: Three People, Three Routes
body.scenario: It is February 2027. Three people come to you about FY 2025-26. Manish never filed at all, and ₹18,000 of TDS on his FD interest is refundable to him. Sneha filed on time in July 2026 but has just found that she claimed a deduction she was not eligible for, which means she owes about ₹12,000 more. Karan filed for FY 2023-24 but never disclosed the gains on US shares he sold that year, and now wants to set it right.
body.prompt: What can each of them do, and what does it cost?
body.modelAnswer: Manish is in the worst position. The belated deadline of 31 December 2026 has passed, so he cannot file a normal return for FY 2025-26 any more. An updated return will not help him, because it cannot be used to claim a refund. His only route is a condonation of delay application to the department, which is discretionary, so his ₹18,000 may simply be lost. Sneha is fine: the revision window runs to 31 March 2027, so she files a revised return, removes the wrong deduction, pays the ₹12,000 with interest, and there is no late fee. Filing voluntarily now is far better than waiting for the department to spot it. Karan is past revision for FY 2023-24, which was AY 2024-25, so his route is an updated return in Form ITR-U. In February 2027 he is between 12 and 24 months from the end of that assessment year, so he pays tax and interest plus 50% additional tax. He should act quickly, since crossing 24 months raises it to 60%. Foreign assets carry their own disclosure obligations and penalties, so this is a case to take to a qualified professional rather than handle alone.

body.title: The Deadline You Cannot Miss
body.textWithBlank: For FY 2025-26, the last date to file a belated return is 31 ___ 2026.
body.explanation: 31 December 2026 is the end of the road for filing a normal return for FY 2025-26. Revision stays open until 31 March 2027, but only for people who filed something.

body.title: If You Have Missed Something, Work Through This
steps: Check whether you filed an original return for the year at all
If you did not, and the belated deadline has not passed, file the belated return now and accept the fee
If you did file, check whether the revision window is still open, and prefer a revised return over everything else
If both windows have closed, check whether an updated return would result in extra tax; if it would only give you a refund, it is not available
Work out which additional tax band you fall into, and file before the band changes
Pay tax, interest and additional tax before filing, and e-verify within 30 days
Take professional advice for foreign assets, business income or large amounts

points: Belated returns for FY 2025-26 can be filed until 31 December 2026 under Section 263(4) of the 2025 Act (139(4) of the 1961 Act), with a late fee of up to ₹5,000, 1% a month interest, no old regime and no carry-forward of most losses
Revised returns under Section 263(5) (139(5)) are open until 31 March 2027 for AY 2026-27, cost nothing by themselves, and can be filed more than once, including for a belated return
The revision window outlasts the belated window, so a mistake found in early 2027 can still be fixed if you filed something
Updated returns under Section 263(6) (139(8A)) run 48 months, to 31 March 2031 for AY 2026-27, with additional tax of 25%, 50%, 60% or 70% of tax plus interest depending on when you file
An updated return can only increase your tax; it cannot claim a refund, reduce tax or report a loss, and only one is allowed per assessment year
If you never filed and are only owed a refund, missing 31 December closes every normal route, leaving only a discretionary condonation request

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax advice. Deadlines, fees and additional tax rates reflect the position for AY 2026-27 at the time of writing and can change through the Finance Act or CBDT notifications. Conditions for updated returns and condonation requests are detailed and fact-specific, so consult a qualified tax professional before acting.
